Li K, Luo H, Huang L, Luo H, Zhu X. Cancer Cell Int. 2020;20:16

flags.appAction: Lesson mdx-hereditary-lynch-men2-brca teaches MSI-H as a screen followed by BRAF V600E and MLH1 methylation testing before germline testing, and explains why mononucleotide panels or four-protein IHC are preferred (accuracy flags f-ch78-msi-not-lynch, f-ch78-msi-panel).

flags.issue: Hit 7 calls RET codon 634 the most common MEN 2A mutation and gives codon 918 in >95% of MEN 2B. Raue 2018 calls 634 the classical high-risk MEN 2A codon and says it was previously the most common. It reports that, since routine RET sequencing of all MTC patients began, more patients have been found with moderate-risk exon 13-15 mutations. The 2015 ATA guideline (the part read) says about 95% of MEN 2B patients carry M918T, while Raue 2018 says >95%. Whether 634 is still the most common rests on one review and has not been checked against a primary series.

evidence.citation: Raue F, Frank-Raue K. J Endocr Soc. 2018;2(8):933-943
Wells SA, Asa SL, Dralle H, et al. Thyroid. 2015;25(6):567-610

flags.appAction: Lesson mdx-hereditary-lynch-men2-brca teaches codon 634 as the classical MEN 2A (ATA-high) codon, notes that moderate-risk mutations are now found more often, and gives M918T as about 95% (ATA) or >95% (Raue) of MEN 2B (accuracy flag f-ch78-ret-634).

flags.issue: Hit 15 says F. tularensis shows no growth on sheep blood agar and pinpoint colonies on chocolate agar in 3-5 days. The ASM sentinel guideline says it may grow at first on blood agar (scant growth) but can fail on subculture because it needs cysteine, and that on cysteine-supplemented agar such as chocolate the colonies are usually too small to see at 24 h but are about 1-2 mm after 48 h or more. Gavina 2023 also describes scant growth of tiny colonies on blood agar after 48 h. The 7-day hold is supported for tissue specimens.

evidence.citation: American Society for Microbiology. Sentinel Level Clinical Laboratory Guidelines for Suspected Agents of Bioterrorism and Emerging Infectious Diseases: Francisella tularensis. Revised March 2016
Gavina K, Whitacre BE, Meyer TL, et al. J Clin Microbiol. 2023;61(6):e0078722

flags.appAction: Lesson micro-specimen-id-transport-biosafety teaches scant growth on blood agar and 1-2 mm chocolate colonies after 48 h or more, and does not teach 'no growth' or '3-5 days'.

flags.issue: Hit 32 says to label BEFORE collection and also to never pre-label tubes, which conflict. Published guidance also differs: the CLSI venipuncture procedure labels tubes after filling, WHO and SIBioC mandate labelling before filling, and the EFLM WG-PRE leaves the choice to local risk analysis while always checking identity in the patient's presence. The two-identifier rule matches the US Joint Commission goal (EFLM asks for at least two, preferably three). Philippine rules are not covered.

evidence.citation: Lippi G, Chiozza L, Mattiuzzi C, Plebani M. J Med Biochem. 2017;36(2):107-112

flags.appAction: Lesson micro-specimen-id-transport-biosafety teaches that pre-labelling guidance differs and keeps the agreed core: two identifiers, never the room, identity checked with the patient present.

flags.issue: Hit 32 says an unlabeled or mislabeled specimen is rejected and recollected. That holds for specimens that can be recollected, but restrictive acceptance policies can allow documented exceptions for irretrievable specimens (CSF, tissue, pre-antibiotic blood cultures), where the collector identifies the specimen in person at the laboratory and signs. The evidence is one hospital's published policy.

evidence.citation: Ning HC, Lin CN, Chiu DT, et al. PLoS One. 2016;11(8):e0160821

flags.appAction: Lesson micro-specimen-id-transport-biosafety teaches reject-and-recollect and notes the policy exception for irretrievable specimens.

flags.issue: Hit 34 places suspected tuberculosis and dimorphic fungi at BSL-3 without separating specimens from cultures. CDC 2012 allows non-aerosol procedures on TB specimens in a BSL-2 laboratory (in a BSC, with coat and gloves), with specimen decontamination, culture propagation and culture manipulation at BSL-3. For identified Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides and Paracoccidioides, it recommends BSL-3 practices and facilities for mould-form cultures. For select agents such as F. tularensis, the ASM sentinel guideline is itself mixed: Section II.A allows BSL-2 practices for clinical specimens, while Section II.B asks for BSL-3 or BSL-2 with BSL-3 precautions in a Class II BSC, so the reviewer's BSL-3 placement there is defensible. These are US (CDC/BMBL/ASM) rules; Philippine rules are not covered.

evidence.citation: Miller JM, Astles R, Baszler T, et al. MMWR Suppl. 2012;61(1):1-102
American Society for Microbiology. Sentinel Level Clinical Laboratory Guidelines for Suspected Agents of Bioterrorism and Emerging Infectious Diseases: Francisella tularensis. Revised March 2016

flags.appAction: Lesson micro-specimen-id-transport-biosafety teaches BSC handling of TB specimens with BSL-3 for TB decontamination and culture work, BSL-3 for dimorphic mould cultures, and a Class II BSC with BSL-3 precautions for suspected Francisella.

flags.issue: Hit 12 states that eosinophils kill helminths via major basic protein. Rosenberg 2013 says this view came largely from tissue histology and from in vitro studies showing antiparasitic activity of MBP and ECP, which are toxic to Schistosoma mansoni schistosomules and larvae. However, changing eosinophil numbers in mouse S. mansoni models did not change disease. In Strongyloides and Angiostrongylus models, removing eosinophils let tissue larvae survive longer. Rosenberg calls the role of eosinophils in mouse helminth models unclear and controversial. Killing via MBP should be taught as in vitro toxicity with an uncertain in vivo role.

evidence.citation: Rosenberg HF, Dyer KD, Foster PS. Nat Rev Immunol. 2013;13(1):9-22

flags.appAction: Lesson heme-eosinophil-il5-tpo-megakaryocytes teaches IL-5 as the key eosinophil factor, with IL-3 and GM-CSF, teaches MBP toxicity as in vitro only, and states that the in vivo role is unclear (lesson flag f-mbp-helminth).

flags.issue: The Trap 5 dodge ('think helminths, not just hay fever') points the right way but leaves something out. Charcot-Leyden crystals are galectin-10, which is also present in basophils and macrophages. They are reported in helminth lesions and also in asthma sputum, allergic fungal sinusitis, allergic rhinitis, tumours and leukaemia. They mark eosinophil-rich inflammation, not one cause. Eosinophilia is more often due to infection in tropical areas and to inflammation in industrialised regions.

evidence.citation: Su J. Molecules. 2018;23(11):2931
Thomsen GN, et al. Front Oncol. 2023;13:1193730

flags.appAction: Lesson heme-eosinophil-il5-tpo-megakaryocytes teaches CLCs as a marker of eosinophil-rich inflammation from many causes, helminths included (lesson flag f-clc-nonspecific).

flags.issue: Trap 6 states that TPO is inversely proportional to platelet mass. Hitchcock 2021 says plasma TPO is usually inversely proportional to platelet count and that how the liver senses platelets is controversial, with two models: platelets soaking up TPO through MPL, and desialylated platelets signalling through hepatic Ashwell-Morell receptors to raise THPO transcription. The trap's examples ('giant platelets', MPN) were not verified in an open source. A verified example of a normal count with abnormal megakaryocytes is the classic 5q- syndrome, which since WHO 2008 is a subset of MDS with isolated del(5q). It is described with macrocytic anaemia, a normal to raised platelet count and hypolobulated megakaryocytes. Across MDS in general, more micromegakaryocytes go with lower platelet counts.

evidence.citation: Hitchcock IS, Hafer M, Sangkhae V, Tucker JA. Platelets. 2021;32(6):770-778
Acha P, Mallo M, Solé F. Cancers (Basel). 2022;14(22):5531
Feng G, et al. Exp Hematol Oncol. 2015;5:12

flags.appAction: Lesson heme-eosinophil-il5-tpo-megakaryocytes teaches the usual inverse TPO-platelet relationship and both sensing models, and uses the classic 5q- syndrome as the normal-count example. Giant platelets and MPN are kept pending (lesson flag f-tpo-inverse).

flags.issue: Hit 5 (and the 'Slope shows strength' memory hook) says the Scatchard plot slope 'gives Ka'. For a plot of B/F against B, the slope is -1/Kd (that is, -Ka) and the x-intercept is the total binding-site concentration, so Ka is the negative of the slope.

evidence.citation: Kastritis PL, Bonvin AM. J R Soc Interface. 2013;10(79):20120835

flags.appAction: Lesson immuno-affinity-precipitin-mab-hapten teaches slope = -Ka and x-intercept = binding sites, and includes a worked calculation.

flags.issue: Hit 4 mentions only antigen excess (which it says 'solubilizes' the precipitate). On the precipitin (Heidelberger) curve, excess antibody and surplus antigen both prevent a visible precipitate, which gives the curve its bell shape. A visible precipitate forms only at the optimal ratio (the zone of equivalence).

evidence.citation: Huber M. Cell Commun Signal. 2013;11(1):7

flags.appAction: Lesson immuno-affinity-precipitin-mab-hapten teaches antibody excess, equivalence and antigen excess as the three zones; the 'solubilizes' wording stays pending.

flags.issue: Exam Trap 4 (and High-Yield Hit 6) say polyclonal serum has 'stronger overall avidity' for complex antigens and that monoclonals distinguish isoenzymes and isotypes. Lipman 2005 calls avidity assay specific (it differs when the same antibodies are used in different techniques). It compares avidity only between classes (decavalent IgM above bivalent IgG), not between polyclonals and monoclonals. Its monoclonal uses are conformational change, phosphorylation states and single members of protein families, and it uses polyclonals for immunoprecipitation of complex antigens. No source read states the avidity or isoenzyme claims.

evidence.citation: Lipman NS, et al. ILAR J. 2005;46(3):258-268

flags.appAction: Lesson immuno-affinity-precipitin-mab-hapten teaches one epitope vs many epitopes and the sourced uses; the avidity and isoenzyme claims stay pending.

flags.issue: Hit 5 calls a PAC/PRA ratio >50 'virtually diagnostic' of primary aldosteronism. No open source read gives this threshold. Ha 2023 says the ratio's specificity rises and its false-positive rate falls as the ratio rises. Ha 2023 and Romero 2016 (summarising the 2016 Endocrine Society guideline) still require confirmatory testing after a positive screen, except when hypokalemia is spontaneous, renin is below detection and PAC is >20 ng/dL.

evidence.citation: Ha J, Park JH, Kim KJ, et al. Endocrinol Metab (Seoul). 2023;38(6):597-618
Romero DG, Yanes Cardozo LL. Int J Endocrinol Metab Disord. 2016;2(3)

flags.appAction: Lesson chem-low-renin-hypertension-aldo teaches the common cut-off of 30 and that a positive screen needs confirmation, and does not teach >50 as diagnostic.

flags.issue: Hit 5 says the ratio counts 'only if PAC itself is elevated too' and states this as a fixed rule. Romero 2016 (2016 Endocrine Society guideline) says to interpret the ratio together with PAC, because a high ratio with a low PAC may only reflect a very low renin. Ha 2023 notes that some investigators add a minimum PAC of >15 ng/dL, and suggests it when renin is excessively suppressed. However, Ha 2023 also reports that 30-40% of ratio-positive PA patients have a PAC below 15 ng/dL. Ratio cut-offs also change with the renin assay (PRA or direct renin concentration) and the units used (Ha 2023 Table 2).

evidence.citation: Ha J, Park JH, Kim KJ, et al. Endocrinol Metab (Seoul). 2023;38(6):597-618
Romero DG, Yanes Cardozo LL. Int J Endocrinol Metab Disord. 2016;2(3)

flags.appAction: Lesson chem-low-renin-hypertension-aldo teaches 'read the ratio with PAC' without a fixed minimum, and says that cut-offs depend on the assay and units.

flags.issue: Trap 6 gives adrenal vein sampling ratios of >4:1 = adenoma and <3:1 = bilateral hyperplasia. For the lateralisation index, Ha 2023 Table 7 gives >=4 with cosyntropin and >=2 without, and Ha 2023's text generally recommends 4 under both conditions. Quencer 2021 tabulates the 2016 Endocrine Society guideline as >4 with cosyntropin and >2 without, and shows cut-offs varying between centres. Ha 2023 describes a grey zone between unilateral and bilateral disease. Lateralisation identifies unilateral disease, which can be an adenoma or unilateral hyperplasia (Romero 2016), not only an adenoma. No source read gives <3 as the cut-off for bilateral disease. The 37.8% CT/MRI-AVS discordance figure (Kempers 2009, 950 patients) is supported as reported by Ha 2023 and Quencer 2021.

evidence.citation: Ha J, Park JH, Kim KJ, et al. Endocrinol Metab (Seoul). 2023;38(6):597-618
Quencer KB. CVIR Endovasc. 2021;4(1):38
Romero DG, Yanes Cardozo LL. Int J Endocrinol Metab Disord. 2016;2(3)

flags.appAction: Lesson chem-low-renin-hypertension-aldo teaches a lateralisation index of 4 or more with cosyntropin as indicating unilateral disease, and the selectivity index for checking cannulation. It does not teach the <3:1 cut-off.

flags.issue: Hit 19 (and the Number Vault) gives 20–25 mg/kg/day as the expected 24-hour creatinine excretion for everyone. Forni Ogna 2015 gives the general nephrology references as 20–25 mg/kg/24 h for men and 15–20 mg/kg/24 h for women. It notes that these come from 1960s–1970s observations in small, mostly selected groups. Applied to a Swiss general population, they would have classed 56% of collections (67% over age 60) as inaccurate. The paper proposes references based on age, sex and BMI.

evidence.citation: Forni Ogna V, et al. BMC Med. 2015;13:40

flags.appAction: Lesson cm-urine-concentration-timed-collections teaches the sex-specific ranges and their age and body-size limits.

flags.issue: Trap 6 and the Number Vault define polyuria as >2.5 L/day. Newell-Price 2025 states that there is no universally accepted definition of polyuria. It reports that past studies used ≥3 L/24 h in adults (≥2 L/m²/24 h in children) or >40 or >50 mL/kg/24 h, and calls ≥3 L/24 h or >40 mL/kg/24 h the least stringent criteria. An adult at 2.5–3 L/day would not meet those criteria. The 2.5 L figure was not found in the sources read.

evidence.citation: Newell-Price J, et al. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2025;110(2):e506-e514

flags.appAction: Lesson cm-urine-concentration-timed-collections teaches that polyuria has no single definition (≥3 L/24 h or >40–50 mL/kg/24 h are used), followed by urine osmolality.

flags.issue: Trap 6 and the Number Vault define oliguria as <400 mL/day and anuria as <100 mL/day. Klein 2018, a narrative review on critically ill patients that follows AKI classification systems, says oliguria is most commonly defined as <0.5 mL/kg/h over 6 h. It notes that other periods (1–24 h) and cutoffs are described. It also separates physiological oliguria (hypovolaemia, fasting, after ultra-endurance events) from pathological oliguria. The mL/day figures were not found in the sources read.

evidence.citation: Klein SJ, et al. J Nephrol. 2018;31(6):855-862

flags.appAction: Lesson cm-urine-concentration-timed-collections teaches the weight-based definition and does not teach <400 or <100 mL/day.

flags.issue: Hit 10 says the first-morning specimen is best for concentration and formed elements. Caleffi 2010 says first-morning urine might be preferred for chemical analysis. For accurate analysis of cell type and morphology (glomerular vs non-glomerular haematuria, atypical cells, decoy cells), it says a second-void specimen might be preferable, because time in the bladder can compromise cell shape and integrity.

evidence.citation: Caleffi A, et al. Biochem Med (Zagreb). 2010;20(2):179-183

flags.appAction: Lesson cm-urine-concentration-timed-collections teaches first-morning urine for chemistry and second-morning urine as possibly better for cell morphology.

flags.issue: Hit 11 (and the Number Vault) lists an albumin concentration of 30–300 mg/L as one of three equivalent windows. Sacks 2011 (Table 8) defines albuminuria only by mg/24 h, µg/min or µg/mg creatinine, and McGill 2022 gives the A1–A3 categories by UACR (A2 30–300 mg/g). Sacks 2011 allows an untimed albumin concentration only for screening, with a cutoff chosen for high sensitivity. The 'earliest sign of diabetic nephropathy' wording also needs qualifying. Sacks 2011 calls albuminuria an early risk marker but notes that low-level albuminuria alone indicates neither kidney disease per se nor progression risk unless hypertension is present, and that about 20% of people progress without it.

evidence.citation: Sacks DB, et al. Diabetes Care. 2011;34(6):e61-e99
McGill JB, et al. BMJ Open Diabetes Res Care. 2022;10(4):e002806

flags.appAction: Lesson cm-urine-concentration-timed-collections teaches the ACR categories and timed equivalents, and does not teach the mg/L window or the 'earliest sign' wording.

flags.issue: Hit 4 says an unexplained osmolal gap means a toxic alcohol until proven otherwise, but it does not cover the negative case. Open sources describe the gap as insensitive, with a wide normal range (quoted as under 10 to under 20 mOsm). The gap shrinks as the alcohol is metabolised to acids, so a normal gap does not exclude toxic alcohol poisoning.

evidence.citation: Gallagher N, Edwards FJ. Adv J Emerg Med. 2019;3(3):e28
Lynd LD, et al. BMC Emerg Med. 2008;8:5

flags.appAction: Lesson chem-toxic-alcohols-salicylate-gaps teaches that a normal osmolal gap does not rule out a toxic alcohol, and lists the other causes of a raised gap.

flags.issue: Hit 15 says tinnitus or hearing loss flags chronic salicylate toxicity. It is well described with chronic therapeutic dosing, but it also occurs after acute single overdoses. In a poison-centre series, tinnitus or hearing loss was documented in 99 of 213 single-overdose cases with a record, and those patients had higher initial and peak salicylate levels. A 2025 review says that in acute salicylism it largely presents as diminished hearing and is not found in all patients. So it is not specific to chronic toxicity, and its absence does not exclude toxicity.

evidence.citation: Samlan SR, et al. West J Emerg Med. 2008;9(3):146-149
Sidlak AM, et al. Cureus. 2025;17(9):e91505

flags.appAction: Lesson chem-toxic-alcohols-salicylate-gaps teaches that tinnitus occurs in acute overdose as well, and that its absence does not exclude toxicity.

flags.issue: Hit 15 says to use the Done nomogram. A 2025 review states that no reliable salicylate nomogram exists, citing a 1989 evaluation of the Done nomogram. It recommends checking further salicylate levels at two-hour intervals and getting a blood gas, because early levels can be undetectable and peaks can be delayed.

evidence.citation: Sidlak AM, et al. Cureus. 2025;17(9):e91505

flags.appAction: Lesson chem-toxic-alcohols-salicylate-gaps does not teach the Done nomogram. It teaches serial levels and blood gases instead.

flags.issue: Hit 11 gives a positive secretin test as a gastrin rise >200 ng/L within 15 min, and the diagnostic pair as fasting gastrin >1000 ng/L with basal acid output >15 mmol/h (plus gastrin >150 ng/L with pH <3 as highly suggestive). Franchina 2024 gives the secretin criterion as a gastrin rise of at least 120 pg/mL (= ng/L) at any sample up to 30 min after 2 U/kg IV secretin. Magi 2023 calls fasting gastrin >10x elevated with gastric pH <2 diagnostic. Rossi 2021 and Franchina 2024 give gastrin >1000 pg/mL with pH <2 as diagnostic. The >150/pH <3 rule was not found (Rossi 2021: normal <100 pg/mL, >300 highly suspicious; Magi 2023 lists basal acid output only as an additional test when gastrin is <10x).

Magi L, et al. Curr Treat Options Oncol. 2023;24(7):725-741
Rossi RE, et al. World J Gastroenterol. 2021;27(35):5890-5907

flags.issue: Hit 9 states 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA is >90% sensitive and >90% specific for carcinoid syndrome. Arasaradnam 2018 (BSG guideline) gives sensitivity and specificity of 88%; Kerolles 2025 cites sensitivity 77% and specificity 97%; Franchina 2024 reports specificity of about 100% but sensitivity of about 35% across NETs. The test remains the recommended biochemical test, but the >90%/>90% figure is not reproduced.

Kerolles M, et al. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2025;110(12):e3980-e3988
Franchina M, et al. Diagnostics (Basel). 2024;14(12):1289

flags.issue: Hit 8 states octreotide controls VIPoma symptoms in >90%. Una Cidon 2022 says somatostatin analogues reduce VIP secretion and that several studies report diarrhoea control in more than 50% of patients, with significant improvement in 25% (its >90% figure refers to tumour-growth inhibition, not symptom control). flags.issue: Gives Crigler-Najjar type I unconjugated bilirubin as '>5, sometimes >20 mg/dL' (repeated in the Number Vault and Table 2). Huang 2022 gives 342–855 µmol/L (about 20–50 mg/dL) for type 1 (UGT1A1 activity 0%) and 103–342 µmol/L (about 6–20 mg/dL) for type 2 (about 10% activity). Values just above 5 mg/dL fit type 2 or Gilbert syndrome (17–103 µmol/L), not type 1.

flags.issue: States that light photoisomerization increases the direct-reacting fraction, so a light-exposed sample can 'manufacture' a conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. In a plasma stability study using a diazo method, total and direct bilirubin both fell significantly after 48 h under artificial light (delays up to 8 h made no significant difference; light-protected plasma was stable for at least 24 h). In an HPLC comparison study, about 30% of photoproducts reacted as indirect bilirubin in a diazo method, whereas on the Ektachem method they raised the conjugated and unconjugated fractions. A 2025 review notes that photoisomers react in total and direct assays to differing degrees by method. The main in vitro effect is falsely low bilirubin, and the shifts between fractions depend on the method. Both primary studies were read as abstracts only.

Ihara H, et al. Clin Chem. 1992;38(10):2124-2129
Lindqvist D, et al. Int J Mol Sci. 2025;26(21):10791

flags.issue: Hit 12 says 'the variant carriers are the ones who get prolonged apnea from succinylcholine' without separating genotypes. Zencirci 2009 reports that heterozygotes show at most about 50% prolongation of the block. Panhuizen 2010 reports that homozygous atypical patients (DN 30 or less) have a markedly prolonged block lasting hours. Delacour 2014 states that prolonged block occurs with marked deficiency (impairment over 70%). The clinically serious risk sits mainly with homozygotes and compound genotypes, although Zencirci also notes that one or more atypical alleles can prolong mivacurium paralysis.

flags.issue: Hit 9 and Exam Trap 6 say Prader-Willi and Angelman result from the SAME 15q11.2 deletion. The EMQN/ACGS guideline gives the imprinted region as 15q11q13. It shows deletion in only 70-75% of PWS (maternal UPD 25-30%, imprinting defect ~1%) and ~75% of AS (UBE3A variant 5-10%, imprinting defect ~3%, paternal UPD 1-2%, unexplained 10-15%). DNA methylation analysis, not deletion FISH, is the confirming test. Exam Trap 6 is also affected.

flags.issue: Hit 12 calls Williams syndrome an ELN deletion at 7q11.23. Sources describe a contiguous gene microdeletion, ~1.55 Mb in ~90% of patients, in a 7q11.23 region of about 28 genes that includes ELN. ELN hemizygosity explains the arteriopathy, but ELN variants alone cause supravalvar aortic stenosis (elastin arteriopathy) without the full Williams-Beuren syndrome.

evidence.citation: Honjo RS, et al. Biomed Res Int. 2015;2015:903175
Stephens SB, et al. J Am Heart Assoc. 2024;13(8):e034048

flags.appAction: Lesson mdx-imprinting-microdeletion-syndromes teaches Williams-Beuren as a contiguous deletion that includes ELN.

flags.issue: Hit 15 says ~1 in 3 children with aniridia develop Wilms tumor. No source read gives this figure. Hol 2021 gives a 45-60% Wilms tumor risk in WAGR, which requires both WT1 and PAX6 in the 11p13 deletion, and says isolated PAX6 deletions carry no Wilms risk. Risk depends on WT1 involvement, not on aniridia alone.

Duffy KA, et al. Front Pediatr. 2021;9:733018

flags.issue: Hit 1 says the start codon is 'always AUG'. Vitale 2025 says an open reading frame 'typically' starts with AUG, and Kearse 2017 says translation can start at non-AUG near-cognate codons (CUG, GUG, UUG) at much lower efficiency, with ribosome profiling showing thousands of such start sites. AUG is still the right exam answer for 'the start codon', but 'always' overstates it.

evidence.citation: Kearse MG, Wilusz JE. Genes Dev. 2017;31(17):1717-1731
Vitale E, et al. IUBMB Life. 2025;77(6):e70031

flags.issue: Hit 14 and Exam Trap 4 say Duchenne = frameshift deletion and Becker = in-frame deletion, with no exceptions. Aartsma-Rus 2016 says close to 10% of mutations do not follow the reading-frame rule (some in-frame changes cause Duchenne, some out-of-frame changes cause Becker). It also says Duchenne comes from out-of-frame duplications (about 11% of patients) and from small mutations (about 20%), including nonsense point mutations that create a premature stop codon, not only from deletions.

evidence.citation: Aartsma-Rus A, et al. J Med Genet. 2016;53(3):145-151

flags.appAction: Lesson mdx-mutation-types-reading-frame-repair teaches the reading-frame rule with its roughly 10% exceptions, and teaches duplications and nonsense mutations as Duchenne causes.

flags.issue: Hit 15 and its memory hook ('NER defect = xeroderma pigmentosum') equate xeroderma pigmentosum with a nucleotide excision repair defect. Leung 2022 says XPA-XPG act in NER, but the XP variant (XPV, about 30% of cases worldwide) has normal NER and mutations in DNA polymerase eta, which performs translesion synthesis past unrepaired UV damage. NER defect remains the best single answer for classic XP, but not every XP patient has defective NER.

evidence.citation: Leung AK, et al. Drugs Context. 2022;11:2022-2-5

flags.appAction: Lesson mdx-mutation-types-reading-frame-repair teaches xeroderma pigmentosum as mostly an NER defect and notes the XP variant form (normal NER, defective polymerase eta).

flags.issue: Hit 11 (and Exam Trap 3) says a disclaimer must be added to the final report of any test not cleared by the FDA. The federal rule found, 21 CFR 809.30(e), requires a specific statement for in-house tests developed using analyte-specific reagents: 'This test was developed and its performance characteristics determined by (Laboratory Name). It has not been cleared or approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.' The rule says the statement is not needed when results come from the cleared or approved test. No source was found requiring it for every non-cleared test.
flags.appAction: Lesson mdx-reimbursement-fda-status-disclaimer teaches the ASR rule, its exact wording and when it does not apply.

flags.issue: Trap 3 (and Hit 11) is right that FDA clearance is not a billing requirement, but it leaves out that payment depends on the payer's coverage. Medicare contractors can cover laboratory-developed tests (the MolDx program evaluates them for coverage and reimbursement), but some coverage policies depend on FDA status: as the AMP report describes it, Medicare's 2018 national coverage determination for next-generation sequencing covered FDA-approved or cleared NGS companion-diagnostic assays in advanced-stage cancer and left NGS tests not approved by the FDA to local contractors. Under CLIA, a test not subject to FDA clearance also needs the lab to establish its own performance specifications before reporting patient results.

evidence.citation: Sireci AN, et al. J Mol Diagn. 2020;22(8):975-993

flags.appAction: Lesson mdx-reimbursement-fda-status-disclaimer teaches that a non-cleared test can be billed, that payment depends on coverage, and that CLIA requires the lab to establish performance.

flags.issue: Hit 10 presents reimbursement as a fixed sequence: coverage, then coding, then payment. The AMP Economics 101 report says that once a code exists, coverage and pricing are set by separate processes, and that NCDs and LCDs define the clinical scenario for coverage, paired with ICD-10 and CPT codes. So the three are separate questions, not a strict one-way order. The point that payment need not match cost is supported: Medicare rates are the volume-weighted median of private-payer rates, or are set by crosswalk or gapfill.

evidence.citation: Sireci AN, et al. J Mol Diagn. 2020;22(8):975-993

flags.appAction: Lesson mdx-reimbursement-fda-status-disclaimer teaches coding, coverage and payment as three separate questions and explains how payment rates are set.

US LDT policy has also changed: the May 2024 FDA LDT rule was vacated by a federal district court on 31 March 2025, and an FDA final rule effective 19 September 2025 reverted 21 CFR 809.3. Philippine regulation and reimbursement are not covered.

flags.issue: Hit 16 gives a 1–6 h onset for staphylococcal food poisoning. Open reviews give 2–8 h (Argudín 2010) and 'usually 3–5 hours', depending on the amount of toxin eaten (Kadariya 2014). The emetic B. cereus window (15 min–6 h) and the diarrhoeal window (about 8–16 h) match Dietrich 2021.

flags.issue: Hit 25 says non-lactose-fermenting (colourless) MacConkey colonies + bloody diarrhoea = Shigella. Some enteroinvasive E. coli strains closely resemble Shigella: they are usually non-motile, lactose-negative and lysine-decarboxylase-negative, and they cause dysentery by the same mode of invasion. S. sonnei ferments lactose slowly. Salmonella enterica is typically lactose-negative. IDSA 2017 lists many causes of visible blood in stool (STEC, Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, E. histolytica, non-cholera Vibrio, Yersinia and others). In a systematic review of children (1977–2016), dysentery identified only 1.9–85.9% of confirmed Shigella infections.

flags.appAction: Lesson micro-food-poisoning-shigella-hpylori teaches the colourless colony as presumptive and requires full identification before Shigella is reported.

flags.issue: Hit 41 says the Kauffmann-White serotype 'drives outbreak tracking and reporting'. Serotyping by O and H antigen agglutination is the first-line characterisation and the basis of surveillance. Diep 2019 states it does not give enough discrimination for outbreak investigation, and molecular subtyping or WGS is used to link cases. The scheme is also called White-Kauffmann-Le Minor.

evidence.citation: Diep B, et al. Front Microbiol. 2019;10:2554
Ibrahim GM, Morin PM. Front Microbiol. 2018;9:2993

flags.appAction: Lesson micro-food-poisoning-shigella-hpylori teaches serotype as the first step and molecular subtyping/WGS for case linkage.

flags.issue: Hit 41 lists the urea breath test, stool antigen and rapid urease test together without saying what each one detects. The breath test and rapid urease test detect urease activity, while the stool antigen test is an immunoassay for H. pylori antigens. The hit also does not say that PPIs lower the accuracy of these tests and should be stopped 14 days before testing (unless PCR is used), or that antibiotics and bismuth should be avoided for 4 weeks. The washout intervals come from one national consensus (Ireland 2024), so they are guideline-dependent. For context, serology (not in the hit) cannot distinguish active from past infection.

Dore MP, Pes GM. J Clin Med. 2021;10(10):2091

flags.appAction: Lesson micro-food-poisoning-shigella-hpylori separates urease-based tests from the stool antigen immunoassay and serology, and teaches the PPI and antibiotic/bismuth washout rules.

flags.issue: Hit 7 says 'vaccine + HBIG within 12 hours of birth' without saying which infants. ACIP 2018 gives both within 12 h to infants of HBsAg-positive mothers and to infants under 2,000 g whose mother's status is unknown. Unknown-status infants of 2,000 g or more get the vaccine within 12 h, and HBIG as soon as possible, no later than 7 days, if the mother turns out to be HBsAg positive. Medically stable infants of 2,000 g or more born to HBsAg-negative mothers get the vaccine alone within 24 h. These are US recommendations; Philippine rules are not covered.

evidence.citation: Schillie S, et al. MMWR Recomm Rep. 2018;67(1):1-31

flags.appAction: Lesson micro-hbv-perinatal-hcv-cure-rubella teaches the rule by maternal HBsAg status and birth weight, plus infant follow-up testing at 9-12 months.

flags.issue: Hits 7 and 15 (perinatal HBV prophylaxis; MMR after delivery for a rubella IgG-negative pregnant woman) match US ACIP recommendations: Schillie 2018 for HBV, and McLean 2013 for rubella (IgG-only prenatal screen, no MMR in pregnancy, vaccinate before discharge, avoid pregnancy for 28 days). Philippine Department of Health schedules were not reviewed and are not covered.

evidence.citation: McLean HQ, et al. MMWR Recomm Rep. 2013;62(RR-04):1-34
Schillie S, et al. MMWR Recomm Rep. 2018;67(1):1-31

flags.appAction: Lesson micro-hbv-perinatal-hcv-cure-rubella teaches the US ACIP rules and labels them as US-only.

flags.issue: Describes LGV only as painless ulcer → suppurative buboes (“groove sign”) → fibrosis/strictures. CDC 2021 states that proctocolitis after rectal exposure is the most common LGV presentation (it can mimic inflammatory bowel disease and, if not treated early, lead to chronic colorectal fistulas and strictures). The inguinal picture (tender, typically unilateral inguinal or femoral lymphadenopathy, with possible buboes) is described as common among heterosexuals. The inoculation ulcer or papule is self-limited and has often disappeared by presentation, and rectal LGV can be asymptomatic. The 21-day doxycycline course is confirmed. “Groove sign” and “painless” were not found in the sources read.

evidence.citation: Workowski KA, et al. MMWR Recomm Rep. 2021;70(4):1-187

flags.appAction: Lesson micro-chlamydia-treatment-lgv teaches proctocolitis as the most common presentation, unilateral inguinal/femoral nodes with buboes and doxycycline 21 days; groove sign and painless wording not taught.

flags.issue: States that C. trachomatis causes 30–50% of NGU in men and that 85–90% of infected men are asymptomatic. CDC 2021 says C. trachomatis is a well-established NGU cause but accounts for fewer than 50% of cases overall, with prevalence varying across populations (M. genitalium 10–25%, T. vaginalis 1–8%, no pathogen in about half). This is consistent with the reviewer's upper bound but does not confirm the 30% lower bound. CDC also says asymptomatic infection is common in men and women without giving a percentage. The 85–90% figure was not confirmed in the sources read.

evidence.citation: Workowski KA, et al. MMWR Recomm Rep. 2021;70(4):1-187

flags.appAction: Lesson micro-chlamydia-treatment-lgv teaches the CDC wording (fewer than half of NGU; asymptomatic infection common) and does not teach the 30–50% or 85–90% figures.

flags.issue: US-specific regulatory content: the two FDA-cleared extragenital NAATs and the claim that no LGV-specific NAAT is FDA cleared. The FDA 2019 release confirms Aptima Combo 2 and Xpert CT/NG as the first devices cleared for throat and rectal testing. CDC 2021 says NAAT detects both LGV and non-LGV strains, that a definitive LGV diagnosis needs LGV-specific molecular testing, and (proctitis section) that molecular testing for LGV is not widely available or not FDA cleared. This supports the reviewer as of 2021. Later clearances were not checked, so “the two” and “none FDA cleared” may be out of date. Philippine regulatory status is not covered.

flags.issue: The reviewer states that all fully automated chemistry analyzers sample directly from the collection tube. Armbruster 2014 lists aliquoting of primary sample tubes among automation functions and states that the laboratory automation system should determine the number of aliquots and sample volume for each specimen, so analyzers do not always sample from the primary tube. The disposable-tip and probe back-flushing carryover controls were not found in the sources read; a washing step between sample dispensing is supported.

flags.issue: The reviewer gives MALDI-TOF '90% species / 98% genus specificity'. This single figure was not found in the reviews read. Hou 2019 tabulates correct-identification rates that vary by organism group (from 98.2% species and 99.8% genus for aerobic Gram-negative isolates down to 62.8% species and 87.3% genus for mycobacteria in one study). Calderaro 2024 describes manufacturer score thresholds (Bruker Biotyper >=2.0 species, 1.7-2.0 genus, <1.7 unreliable). These are identification rates, not specificity. Known limits include E. coli vs Shigella and S. pneumoniae vs S. mitis/oralis.

evidence.citation: Calderaro A, Chezzi C. Microorganisms. 2024;12(2):322
Hou TY, Chiang-Ni C, Teng SH. J Food Drug Anal. 2019;27(2):404-414

flags.appAction: Lesson ops-analyzer-carryover-immunoassay-maldi teaches score thresholds and limitations and does not teach a single percentage figure.

flags.issue: Hit 8 (repeated in the Number Vault and a Memory Hook) says 10–20% of Kawasaki disease patients still develop coronary sequelae despite IVIG plus aspirin. The Italian Society of Pediatrics guideline reports coronary artery aneurysms in about 15–25% of untreated patients and in less than 5% of patients treated with IVIG within 10 days of fever onset. The guideline's 15–20% figure is the IVIG-resistance rate. The reviewer may be counting coronary dilation or late-treated or IVIG-resistant patients, which the guideline does not quantify.

evidence.citation: Marchesi A, et al. Ital J Pediatr. 2018;44(1):102

flags.appAction: Lesson immuno-medium-vessel-pan-kawasaki teaches coronary aneurysms in 15–25% untreated vs <5% with IVIG within 10 days, plus IVIG resistance of about 15–20%. The reviewer figure is kept pending.

flags.issue: Hit 8 and the Number Vault present NT-proBNP 235.2 pg/mL as the cutoff that distinguishes Kawasaki disease from other febrile illnesses. In the Lin 2015 meta-analysis, 235.2 was the cutoff of a single study (Cho 2011: sensitivity 0.66, specificity 0.77). Study cutoffs ranged from 98 to 260 pg/mL across different assays, pooled NT-proBNP sensitivity was 0.89 and specificity 0.72, and the authors could not conclusively suggest a best cutoff.

evidence.citation: Lin KH, et al. BMJ Open. 2015;5(4):e006703

flags.appAction: Lesson immuno-medium-vessel-pan-kawasaki teaches NT-proBNP as a supportive test with study-dependent cutoffs (98–260 pg/mL). An exam trap says a 235.2 pg/mL value does not confirm KD.

flags.issue: Hit 12 says HBV accounted for more than one third of adult PAN cases in the pre-vaccination era. The open review read (Pașa 2023) says up to 30% of PAN cases were caused by HBV, now less than 5%. Both sources agree on the current figure of under 5%. The historical share depends on era and cohort, and the original cohort data were not read.

evidence.citation: Pașa V, et al. Medicina (Kaunas). 2023;59(6):1162

flags.appAction: Lesson immuno-medium-vessel-pan-kawasaki teaches 'up to 30% historically, now under 5%'. The reviewer's '>1/3' is kept pending.

flags.issue: Hit 4 calls 22% PE->PE-Cy5 subtraction correct 'in the example', with 15% as under and 26% as over. Memory Hook 4 ('22 is the magic spillover number') and the Number Vault ('22% is the textbook PE->PE-Cy5 compensation') turn this into a general value. No source read gives a standard value. EuroFlow (Kalina 2012) says compensation values depend on the dyes, the optical filters, the signal intensity and the PMT voltage. It needed reagent-specific compensation controls for tandem conjugates such as PE-Cy7 and APC-H7, and 405-nm laser power failures forced new instrument setup and compensation. Bhowmick 2021 shows that spillover spread values depend on detector sensitivity. The numbers work only as a worked example.

evidence.citation: Kalina T, et al. Leukemia. 2012;26(9):1986-2010
Bhowmick D, et al. Sci Rep. 2021;11(1):20553

flags.appAction: Lesson heme-flow-compensation-tandem-fmo teaches 22/15/26% only as a worked example and states that spillover is measured per instrument and, for tandems, per reagent.

flags.issue: Hit 11 says PE-Cy5 can emit as APC under red-laser excitation and APC-Cy7 can emit as APC, and calls both 'variable parent emission'. The sources describe two different mechanisms. Le Roy 2009 (abstract) found that APC-Cy7/H7 tandems degrade over time through a cell-dependent mechanism, which gives a nonspecific signal in the APC (donor) channel. Kalina 2012 likewise describes tandems giving variable spillover into the donor-dye channel. Bhowmick 2023 says PE-Cy5 and APC have similar emission maxima, so cross-laser bleedthrough into the APC detector is expected. That is spillover, not emission from the parent (donor) dye PE.

evidence.citation: Le Roy C, et al. Cytometry A. 2009;75(10):882-890
Bhowmick D, et al. Immunohorizons. 2023;7(12):819-833
Kalina T, et al. Leukemia. 2012;26(9):1986-2010

flags.appAction: Lesson heme-flow-compensation-tandem-fmo teaches APC-Cy7/H7 degradation (donor APC signal) and PE-Cy5 signal reaching the APC detector as separate mechanisms.

flags.issue: Hit 12 (and Exam Trap 4) say Tier 1/2 codes exclude pre-extraction procedures like microdissection, which are separately billable. The Medicare NCCI Policy Manual (Ch. X, section F) says molecular pathology codes include all aspects of sample preparation, cell lysis, internal measures to assure adequate DNA/RNA (quantitation included, not billed as 84311) and the assay, and that scraping tumor off an unstained slide is included and must not be reported as microdissection (88380/88381). Microdissection codes describe sample preparation of microscopically identified target cells. The blanket 'pre-extraction = separately billable' needs this qualification.

evidence.citation: CMS. Medicare NCCI Policy Manual, Chapter X: Pathology/Laboratory Services. Revision 1/1/2024

flags.appAction: Lesson mdx-cpt-molecular-tiers-unlisted-bundling teaches that slide scraping and quantitation are included in the molecular code and that true microdissection has its own codes (88380, 88381).

flags.issue: Trap 2 (and Hit 7) present 81479 as the code for any test not in Tier 1 or Tier 2. Other category I code families (genomic sequencing procedure panels such as 81445/81450/81455, multianalyte assays) and proprietary laboratory analysis codes must be checked first; 81479 is used only when no existing code appropriately describes the service, generally needs documentation of the procedure and medical necessity, and the claim is denied if an appropriate code exists. For a multigene NGS test with no fitting code, NCCI allows 81479 (one unit) or component codes when medically reasonable and necessary.

CMS. Medicare NCCI Policy Manual, Chapter X: Pathology/Laboratory Services. Revision 1/1/2024

flags.appAction: Lesson mdx-cpt-molecular-tiers-unlisted-bundling teaches 81479 only when no code of any family fits, usually with documentation.

So 2013 is when Medicare adopted the new codes and retired the stacked code, while the codes themselves were first published in January 2012.

flags.issue: Ch. 57 Hit 31 gives cryptococcal induction as amphotericin B + flucytosine and says fluconazole is for consolidation/maintenance. That is true of fluconazole alone. But the WHO 2022 preferred induction is a single high dose (10 mg/kg) of liposomal amphotericin B plus 14 days of flucytosine and fluconazole 1200 mg/day (the AMBITION regimen), and several WHO alternatives also use fluconazole during induction. Consolidation is fluconazole 800 mg/day and maintenance 200 mg/day.

Chronic hyperplastic candidiasis, however, forms plaques that cannot be removed by gentle scraping, so a fixed white plaque is not automatically OHL. EBV in situ hybridisation is the gold-standard confirmation (only 20 of 28 clinically suspected lesions were confirmed in one series).

flags.issue: Ch. 57 Hit 34 describes Rhizopus/mucormycosis hyphae as aseptate and implies that rhizoids identify Rhizopus. Sources describe Mucorales hyphae as aseptate or pauciseptate: they are coenocytic, and septa can form in tissue but not at regular distances. So a few septa do not exclude a mucormycete. Mucor species can also form rhizoids, although in Rhizopus the rhizoids are formed opposite the sporangiophores.

flags.issue: Hit 5 (and Exam Trap 6 and the Number Vault) give ADAMTS13 activity '≤5–10%' for TTP and 'normal/mildly decreased (30–100%)' for HUS. It says to consider HUS when activity is above 10% after excluding other secondary causes of TMA. It gives no 30% lower bound for HUS. One Korean aHUS registry cohort (defined by activity >10%) had a median of 77%. The reviewer's 30–100% band leaves 10–30% unassigned and is not a guideline cut-off.

flags.issue: Hit 15 says destructive causes (ITP/TTP/HIT) show increased megakaryocytes from compensatory production. One single-centre study found more marrow megakaryocytes in adult ITP, but its ITP criteria already required normal or increased megakaryocytes. The Spanish GEPTI recommendations note that ITP autoantibodies also reduce platelet production by blocking TPO function and increasing megakaryocyte apoptosis, so ITP is not purely destructive. No open source was read that supports the claim for TTP or HIT. The chemotherapy (production failure) half is mostly supported, but Kuter 2022 notes that not all chemotherapy drugs reduce production and some increase platelet destruction.

flags.issue: Hit 9 presents mantle cell lymphoma (CD5+, cyclin D1+, t(11;14)) and follicular lymphoma (CD10+, t(14;18)) features as invariant. WHO-HAEM5 (Alaggio 2022) gives IGH::CCND1 in at least 95% of MCL, says about 85% of FL are classic FL carrying t(14;18) IGH::BCL2, and says non-nodal MCL characteristically lacks SOX11 and frequently lacks CD5. Gajzer 2025 gives CD10 expression in about 90% of FL. The classic associations remain the best exam answers, but a missing marker or translocation does not exclude the diagnosis.

flags.issue: Hit 5 and Exam Trap 3 present the amenorrhea workup as a strict five-step order, with FSH/LH checked only after the progestin challenge, and say 'order matters'. Open reviews measure FSH, prolactin and TSH in the first round with hCG. Gibson 2020 (adolescent FHA review) measures FSH, LH, estradiol, prolactin and TSH routinely alongside beta-hCG. Nelson 2023 lists hCG, FSH, prolactin, TSH, testosterone and pelvic ultrasound as the critical initial tests. Gibson 2020 says experts caution against routine use of the progesterone withdrawal challenge because it may be unreliable and is associated with false-negative withdrawals. Nelson 2023 reports a woman later diagnosed with POI who bled after two progestin challenges, which delayed her diagnosis. Testing hCG first still stands. Also applies to Exam Trap 3.

evidence.citation: Sophie Gibson ME, Fleming N, Zuijdwijk C, Dumont T. J Clin Res Pediatr Endocrinol. 2020;12(Suppl 1):18-27
Nelson LM, et al. Front Endocrinol (Lausanne). 2023;14:1227253

flags.issue: Hit 14 labels 12 months amenorrhea + FSH 85 mIU/mL + estradiol <10 pg/mL as 'primary ovarian failure (menopause)' and gives no age. Before age 40 the same pattern is premature ovarian insufficiency. ESHRE 2024 requires only >=4 months of disordered cycles plus an elevated FSH >25 IU/L for that diagnosis, and calls ovarian failure at age 40-44 'early menopause'. Natural menopause is recognised after 12 consecutive months without menstruation with no other cause, and generally occurs at age 45-55 (WHO).

evidence.citation: Panay N, et al. Hum Reprod Open. 2024;2024(4):hoae065
World Health Organization. Menopause [fact sheet]

flags.issue: Hit 14 calls beta-2 transferrin CSF-specific. Oh 2017 still describes it as a highly sensitive and specific CSF marker, so its confirmatory role stands. But Oh 2017 also states that beta-2 transferrin is found in perilymph and vitreous humour, and that eyeball rupture can give a false-positive result for a CSF leak. 'CSF-specific' needs that qualification.

flags.issue: Hit 12 gives meconium a 2nd and 3rd trimester window, which is broadly consistent with the sources. Lange 2014 says meconium formation is generally agreed to begin at about 12 weeks, but some authors suggest up to 20 weeks, so the window has no sharp start. Price 2018 adds that meconium cannot detect first-trimester exposure, may be passed in utero, may contain drugs given during labour, and may be passed late. Maschke 2021 used meconium EtG >=10 ng/g as a marker of third-trimester exposure. The reviewer's general statement that meconium EtG 'documents maternal alcohol use' therefore needs the time-window qualification.

flags.issue: Hit 2 calls inulin clearance the GFR gold standard and gives no context. Speeckaert 2021 describes urinary inulin clearance as the long-standing reference method. It also says most clinicians have abandoned inulin because the procedure is laborious and supply is limited, and that they now use iohexol, iothalamate, 51Cr-EDTA or 99mTc-DTPA clearance to measure GFR. Inulin is still the correct answer to the ideal-marker concept, but it is not what laboratories run routinely.

evidence.citation: Speeckaert MM, et al. J Pers Med. 2021;11(10):949

flags.appAction: Lesson chem-gfr-clearance-creatinine-limits teaches inulin as the classic reference concept (filtered, neither secreted nor reabsorbed) and names the exogenous markers now used for measured GFR.

flags.issue: Trap 6 and the Quick-Compare table present a BUN:creatinine ratio above 20 as favouring volume depletion, or prerenal azotemia over ATN. Uchino 2012 studied 3641 AKI inpatients. About half (53.2%) had a ratio above 20, the distribution was not bimodal, and a high ratio carried higher, not lower, hospital mortality. The authors conclude that using the ratio to separate prerenal azotemia from ATN cannot be justified. They also note that BUN is modulated by parenteral nutrition, protein catabolism, steroid administration and GI bleeding.

evidence.citation: Uchino S, et al. Clin Kidney J. 2012;5(2):187-191

flags.appAction: Lesson chem-gfr-clearance-creatinine-limits teaches a ratio above 20 as suggestive of volume depletion but never proof, and lists the non-renal influences on BUN.

flags.issue: Hit 13 (and Exam Trap 6) state that genotype-guided warfarin dosing did NOT meaningfully improve time in therapeutic range in the big trials, naming Pirmohamed (EU-PACT) among trials with no/minimal benefit. CPIC 2017 reports that COAG showed no difference in time to stable dose or percent time in therapeutic range, but that EU-PACT showed shorter time to stable dose, improved percent time in therapeutic range and fewer INR>4 episodes, and that GIFT revealed a 27% reduction in its composite outcome; CPIC provides genotype-based dosing when results are available. The evidence is mixed rather than uniformly negative.

evidence.citation: Johnson JA, Caudle KE, Gong L, et al. Clin Pharmacol Ther. 2017;102(3):397-404

flags.appAction: Lesson heme-antiplatelet-guided-therapy teaches the warfarin genotype trials as mixed (COAG no TTR gain; EU-PACT better TTR; GIFT 27% fewer composite events) and does not say genotyping never helped.

flags.issue: Hit 10 gives 5-7 days as a fixed figure for aspirin's platelet effect after stopping. A review table (Jourdi 2022, Table 1) does list 5-7 days for time to platelet function recovery after aspirin cessation, but Lee 2014 found arachidonic acid (ASPI) aggregation normalised 96 hours after the last 100 mg dose in hypertensive patients before dental extraction, attributing the faster recovery partly to new platelet production, while the ACCP guidance cited there suggested stopping 7-10 days before noncardiac surgery in low-risk patients. The recovery figure is test-, dose- and population-dependent, not a single number.

Jourdi G, Godier A, Lordkipanidze M, et al. Front Cardiovasc Med. 2022;9:805525

flags.issue: Hit 9 dates the FDA clopidogrel boxed warning to March 2010. CPIC 2022 confirms a boxed warning on diminished effectiveness in CYP2C19 poor metabolizers and states that the FDA updated it in 2016 to cover all patients taking clopidogrel instead of only ACS patients undergoing PCI, but none of the sources read gives a March 2010 date. The warning is also US labelling: Philippine FDA labelling and local guidance are not covered.

flags.issue: Hit 1, Exam Trap 2, the figure caption, the Number Vault ('72-hour rule window 72 h'), the Memory Hook and the chapter Q&A state the rule as a 72-hour window, and the figure ties it to tests 'ordered within 72 hours'. For subsection (d) hospitals paid under IPPS, 42 CFR 412.2(c)(5) and the CMS Three Day Payment Window page count the date of admission plus the 3 calendar days immediately before it. For non-subsection (d) hospitals (psychiatric, rehabilitation, long-term care, children's and cancer hospitals) the CMS page gives the admission date plus 1 day before it. The rule covers services furnished by the hospital or by an entity it wholly owns or wholly operates. Diagnostic services, including clinical lab tests, are always included; nondiagnostic services are included only if related to the admission. Under 42 CFR 414.510(a) a lab test's date of service is normally the specimen collection date, not the order date. So a test collected more than 72 hours before admission can still fall in the window. The reviewer's exclusion of independent nonhospital labs is consistent with the ownership condition.

evidence.citation: 42 CFR § 412.2(c)(5) — Basis of payment (eCFR, version 2026-10-01)
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. Three Day Payment Window. CMS.gov
42 CFR § 414.510 — Laboratory date of service (eCFR, version 2026-10-01)

flags.appAction: Lesson ops-payment-window-opps-clfs teaches the calendar-day window (admission day + 3 calendar days for IPPS hospitals; admission day + 1 day before for non-IPPS hospitals), the ownership/operation condition and the collection-date rule, with a question on a test collected more than 72 hours before admission.

flags.issue: Hit 12 says APCs began in 2000 for hospital outpatient services but clinical lab tests are generally still paid on the CMS fee schedule. The start date holds: 42 CFR 419.1 dates OPPS to services furnished on or after July 1, 2000, and 419.20 states applicability to hospitals from August 1, 2000. 42 CFR 419.22(l) excludes clinical diagnostic laboratory tests from OPPS 'except as provided in § 419.2(b)(17)', and 419.2(b)(17) packages certain clinical diagnostic laboratory tests into the OPPS payment for the related service. The CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual (ch. 16, section 30.3) states that for OPPS hospitals, beginning January 1, 2014, outpatient lab tests are generally packaged as ancillary services and do not receive separate payment. Separate CLFS payment applies when the hospital provides only outpatient lab tests to the patient that day. The fee-schedule statement therefore holds for lab-only hospital outpatient visits (and, per the same section, for independent laboratories and non-patient specimens), but not as the general rule for hospital outpatients who also receive other services.

evidence.citation: 42 CFR §§ 419.2(b)(17) and 419.22(l) — OPPS packaged costs and excluded services (eCFR, version 2026-10-01)
42 CFR §§ 419.1 and 419.20 — OPPS basis and scope; hospitals subject to OPPS (eCFR, version 2026-10-01)
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04), Chapter 16: Laboratory Services, section 30.3 (Rev. 13746, 2026)

flags.appAction: Lesson ops-payment-window-opps-clfs teaches that an OPPS hospital's outpatient lab tests are generally packaged with the other outpatient services that day and are paid separately on the Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule when lab tests are the only outpatient service, with a question on a lab-only visit.

flags.issue: Trap 3 says that reading a low CH50 as complement consumption is a trap, because a low CH50 points to a missing component and consumption shows up as low C3/C4. Ekdahl 2018 says haemolytic assays detect both deficiencies of single components and loss of function from consumption of intact components, and uses them to monitor SLE flares, during which classical-pathway haemolytic function falls as C3, C4 and factor B are used up. It also says severe in vivo consumption must be excluded (by activation products such as C3d,g) before calling a deficiency. A low CH50 fits either cause; component levels and activation products decide which.

evidence.citation: Ekdahl KN, et al. Front Immunol. 2018;9:2237

flags.appAction: Lesson immuno-immune-screens-trec-ch50-spep teaches that a low CH50 can mean deficiency or consumption, with C3/C4, activation products such as C3d,g and single-factor tests deciding which, and carries accuracy flag f-ch50-consumption-trap.

flags.issue: The reviewer says closed-tube real-time PCR 'kills' the nested-PCR contamination problem. Lovatt 2002 says real-time Q-PCR runs in a closed system that removes post-PCR processing and reduces the chance of carryover contamination (not eliminates it), and still calls for strict contamination control. Dunbar 2019 notes that commercial nested and multiplex nested assays have largely overcome the limitations of nested PCR, including the contamination risk of separate tubes, so the downside is tied to open tube transfer rather than to nested PCR itself.

evidence.citation: Lovatt A. J Biotechnol. 2002;82(3):279-300
Dunbar S, Das S. J Clin Virol. 2019;115:18-31

flags.appAction: Lesson mdx-nested-competitive-arms-multiplex-pcr teaches that closed real-time PCR reduces carryover and that commercial nested assays have largely overcome the two-tube limitations.

flags.issue: The reviewer gives allele-specific PCR sensitivity 'down to 0.1% (IDH1, TERT in glioma)'. Huang 2013 reports 0.1-2% for JAK2 V617F ARMS assays and 0.5% for its own BRAF V600E ARMS assay, so the figure depends on the assay; the IDH1/TERT glioma examples were not verified against an open source.

evidence.citation: Huang T, Zhuge J, Zhang WW. Biomark Res. 2013;1(1):3

flags.appAction: Lesson mdx-nested-competitive-arms-multiplex-pcr teaches the 3-prime principle and an assay-dependent ~0.1-2% range; the IDH1/TERT glioma examples are left pending.

flags.issue: Hit 8 (and Trap 4) name Kell as the only antigen lost on DTT-treated reagent cells. Lancman 2018 (Table 2 and text) lists antigens of the Lutheran, Yt, JMH, LW, Cromer, Indian, Dombrock and Knops systems as DTT-denatured too, so antibodies to them (for example anti-Yt) can be missed with this method. The paper's rule is to give Kell-negative red cells unless the patient is known to be Kell-positive.

evidence.citation: Lancman G, Arinsburg S, Jhang J, Cho HJ, Jagannath S, Madduri D, Parekh S, Richter J, Chari A. Front Immunol. 2018;9:2616

flags.issue: Hit 12 presents HLA-G protection of the placenta (maternofetal tolerance) as settled fact. Hunt 2006 writes that many reports link HLA-G to tolerance, but most are associative rather than clearly illustrative of definitive function. HLA-G was first found on extravillous cytotrophoblast and is a ligand for the inhibitory receptors ILT2 and ILT4 (Rebmann 2014), but its causal role in tolerance should be taught as a link, not a proven mechanism.

evidence.citation: Hunt JS, et al. Reprod Biol Endocrinol. 2006;4(Suppl 1):S10
Rebmann V, et al. J Immunol Res. 2014;2014:297073

flags.issue: The Number Vault row on HLA-C expression (about 10-fold lower than HLA-A/-B) gives the cause as 'inefficient association + mutated enhancer A'. McCutcheon 1995 (abstract read; full text is a scanned PDF) found that HLA-C heavy chains associate and dissociate with beta-2 microglobulin at rates comparable to HLA-A and -B, and linked the low surface expression to faster HLA-C mRNA degradation. Kaur 2017 lists inefficient peptide binding or association with chaperones (TAP, tapasin) only as proposed mechanisms. The roughly 10% level is supported (Zemmour 1992), but the mechanism is not settled. The 'mutated enhancer A' part was not checked against any source in this review.

Kaur G, et al. Nat Commun. 2017;8:15924
Zemmour J, Parham P. J Exp Med. 1992;176(4):937-950

flags.issue: Hit 9 gives fluorescence lifetimes of 10⁻⁹–10⁻⁶ s and phosphorescence lifetimes of 10⁻⁴–10 s. Hit 11 gives fluorescein 4.5 ns and Eu³⁺ chelate 10–1000 μs. Open sources give different ranges. Zacharioudaki 2022 gives fluorescence 10⁻¹⁰–10⁻⁷ s and phosphorescence 10⁻⁶ s up to seconds. Kristoffersen 2018 reports that most earlier fluorescein measurements are near 4 ns and itself measured 3.3–3.6 ns, depending on solvent. Hagan 2011 gives lanthanide luminescence in the μs–ms range, which is consistent with the reviewer's Eu³⁺ figure. Exact ranges vary by source, molecule and environment. The qualitative contrast is consistent across sources: fluorescence is singlet and lasts nanoseconds, phosphorescence and lanthanide emission are much slower.

Kristoffersen AS, et al. J Fluoresc. 2018;28(5):1065-1073
Hagan AK, Zuchner T. Anal Bioanal Chem. 2011;400(9):2847-2864

flags.issue: Hit 13 says to freeze platelet-free plasma at -20 C, applies one 4-hour testing limit to every test, and says holding over 4 hours gives low FVIII and vWF. Magnette 2016 prefers storage at -70 C or below, because at -20 C most coagulation parameters stay stable for only about 2 weeks. It gives PT/INR samples about 24 h of stability at room temperature and limits the APTT to 4 h on fresh plasma because labile FVIII (and possibly FV) is lost with delay, so the FVIII part of the hit holds. It reports VWF as stable for 48 h at room temperature and links low FVIII together with low VWF to cold storage of whole blood, not to delay at room temperature.

evidence.citation: Magnette A, et al. Thromb J. 2016;14:49

flags.appAction: Lesson heme-pt-specimen-fvii-vitamin-k teaches -70 C or below as the preferred storage temperature (-20 C for about 2 weeks), different time limits for PT/INR (about 24 h) and APTT (4 h), and cold storage of whole blood as the cause of low FVIII and VWF.

flags.issue: Trap 5 says vitamin K must be given IV slowly (10 mg over 15-30 min) with a 2-4 hour onset. Witt 2016 prefers oral vitamin K for non-bleeding patients with a raised INR, keeps slow IV vitamin K (5-10 mg) together with four-factor PCC for major bleeding, calls subcutaneous vitamin K a last resort, and says new factor synthesis needs at least 6 h and more likely 12-24 h to lower the INR significantly. Vigue 2009 reports that the INR starts to fall within 4 h of IV vitamin K but almost entirely through factor VII. Mathews & Hayward 2025 describe a slow IV infusion over 30 min (no faster than 1 mg/min) for urgent reversal. The sources read did not confirm the 15-minute lower bound.

evidence.citation: Witt DM, et al. J Thromb Thrombolysis. 2016;41(1):187-205
Vigué B. Crit Care. 2009;13(2):209
Mathews N, Hayward CPM. Ann Lab Med. 2025;45(4):358-366

flags.appAction: Lesson heme-pt-specimen-fvii-vitamin-k teaches oral vitamin K as preferred without major bleeding, slow IV vitamin K plus PCC for major bleeding, an early INR fall within about 4 h that is mostly factor VII, and a significant INR fall after at least 6 h (often 12-24 h).

flags.issue: Pairs PV with low EPO and secondary erythrocytosis with high/appropriate EPO as a clean split. In the 2016 WHO criteria a subnormal EPO is only the minor criterion; diagnosis rests on Hb/Hct, marrow panmyelosis and JAK2 V617F/exon 12 (all three major, or the first two plus the minor). Hypoxic secondary erythrocytosis often has a normal (compensated) EPO, EPOR mutations give a subnormal EPO, and about 40% (18 of 44) of JAK2-negative non-neoplastic erythrocytosis in one cohort had EPO below normal, so a low EPO alone does not identify PV.

evidence.citation: Barbui T, et al. Blood Cancer J. 2018;8(2):15
Gangat N, et al. Leukemia. 2021;35(8):2166-2181
Mori Y, et al. Cancer Med. 2023;12(2):1079-1089

flags.issue: Advises checking p50 and arterial O2 saturation when electrophoresis is normal in unexplained erythrocytosis. The source adds that cation-exchange HPLC is normal in about one-third of high-oxygen-affinity variants, so HBB/HBA1/HBA2 sequencing is often needed, and that a low venous p50 (<24 mmHg) also occurs with 2,3-BPG deficiency and methemoglobinemia. The source lists arterial blood gas and overnight oximetry only as initial tests for hypoxia in acquired erythrocytosis; it does not present arterial O2 saturation as a test for a high-affinity variant.

evidence.citation: Gangat N, et al. Leukemia. 2021;35(8):2166-2181

flags.appAction: Lesson heme-erythrocytosis-workup teaches venous p50 <24 mmHg and its three causes, and globin gene sequencing after a normal HPLC. It does not teach arterial O2 saturation.

flags.issue: Hit 4 (and Exam Trap 3) says that duplicating a data element across tables 'breaks referential integrity'. In standard relational-database usage, referential integrity is the foreign-key rule that referencing values must match an existing row in the referenced table. A stale duplicate is a data-consistency (update) problem that a foreign key does not detect. Denormalization trades integrity and consistency for query speed. The reviewer's practical point (keep one home per data element) holds, but the term is used loosely.

evidence.citation: PostgreSQL Global Development Group. PostgreSQL Documentation (current): Section 5.5.5 Foreign Keys; Appendix M Glossary (Referential integrity)
Dilling TJ. Adv Radiat Oncol. 2020;5(6):1280-1285
Angles R, et al. Database (Oxford). 2024;2024:baad093

flags.appAction: Lesson ops-single-source-truth-lis-schema teaches single source of truth, and that a stale duplicate is a consistency failure distinct from a foreign-key (referential integrity) violation. It records lesson flag f-duplication-ri.

flags.issue: Hit 12 says phenytoin, phenobarbital and heavy alcohol 'falsely elevate' GGT. Open sources describe GGT activity as inducible by drugs: carbamazepine, phenobarbital, phenytoin, valproic acid and other medications can raise it, a carbamazepine-related rise is attributed to enzyme induction (increased synthesis) without liver pathology, and GGT is a traditional marker of alcohol consumption. The rise is real (biological), not an analytical false result. The mechanism of the alcohol-related rise was not established in the sources read.

Koenig G, Seneff S. Dis Markers. 2015;2015:818570

flags.issue: Trap 3 calls lipase 'the definitive, specific marker' for pancreatitis (echoed in Hit 12 and the Memory Hook 'Lipase leads; amylase misleads'). The Cochrane review found lipase sensitivity 0.79 and specificity 0.89, against amylase 0.72 and 0.93 (at >3x ULN), could not compare the tests formally because data were sparse, and found that about a quarter of acute pancreatitis cases were missed by these tests. WSES 2019 says lipase is preferred mainly because it is more sensitive and has a longer diagnostic window, and that lipase also rises in renal disease, appendicitis, cholecystitis, chronic pancreatitis and bowel obstruction. The diagnosis needs two of three criteria. The trap's main point, that a normal amylase does not exclude pancreatitis, is supported.

Leppäniemi A, Tolonen M, Tarasconi A, et al. World J Emerg Surg. 2019;14:27

flags.issue: Hit 13 describes fulminant hepatic failure as AST often >10,000 IU/L with AST > ALT, low albumin/protein and high ammonia. Ozturk 2023 (citing AASLD/ACG) and Fernández 2024 define acute liver failure as INR >=1.5 (Fernández: >1.5) plus hepatic encephalopathy in a patient without pre-existing liver disease, with illness under 26 weeks. Aminotransferase height varies widely by cause: paracetamol often >3,500 IU/L, hepatitis B 1,000-2,000 (with ALT usually above AST), acute fatty liver of pregnancy <1,000. Falling aminotransferases while bilirubin and INR rise are a poor sign. High ammonia is supported; low albumin was not found as a feature in the sources read.

evidence.citation: Ozturk NB, Herdan E, Saner FH, Gurakar A. J Clin Med. 2023;12(23):7451
Fernández J, Bassegoda O, Toapanta D, Bernal W. JHEP Rep. 2024;6(9):101131

flags.appAction: Lesson ops-detective-pancreatitis-liver-failure teaches the definition based on INR and encephalopathy and explains that aminotransferase levels vary by cause; it does not teach low albumin.

flags.issue: Hit 9 and Exam Trap 2 call the Weil-Felix test obsolete and say not to use it. Open reviews agree it has poor sensitivity and specificity (spotted fever group: sensitivity 21-70%, specificity 46-96% in Stewart 2021 Table 1; Koh 2010 says the OX-K reaction lacks sensitivity and specificity) and De Vito 2020 says it should no longer be a first-line method, but Stewart 2021 notes it is still the only test available in some resource-limited settings and De Vito 2020 calls it an option in developing countries, which matters for MTLE candidates. Better framing: unreliable, confirm with IFA or PCR where available.

evidence.citation: Stewart AG, Stewart AGA. Pathogens. 2021;10(10):1319
De Vito A, et al. Mediterr J Hematol Infect Dis. 2020;12(1):e2020056
Koh GC, et al. Am J Trop Med Hyg. 2010;82(3):368-370

flags.appAction: Lesson micro-rickettsial-rash-eschar-weil-felix teaches Weil-Felix as unreliable (poor sensitivity and specificity) and to be replaced by IFA or PCR where available, noting continued use in resource-limited settings.

The CDC 2016 guidance gives rash onset as typically 2-4 days after fever onset and describes palm/sole involvement as usually appearing by day 5 or 6 and indicating advanced disease, but gives no percentage for RMSF (it gives about half for Rickettsia parkeri rickettsiosis). The 50% figure needs a source.

flags.issue: Lists oral vancomycin as first-line for C. difficile with fidaxomicin only in brackets. Bainum 2023 reports that the 2017 IDSA/SHEA guideline removed metronidazole as a preferred option for mild CDI and that the 2021 focused update gives fidaxomicin preferred status over vancomycin; oral vancomycin remains endorsed (ACG: fidaxomicin or vancomycin). Gu 2022 (systematic review of guidelines) found 80-100% agreement for vancomycin (10 guidelines) and fidaxomicin (8) in first-episode mild CDI, while metronidazole is still recommended by some guidelines (high agreement in 5 of 9), typically for low-risk disease or when fidaxomicin and vancomycin are limited. The 2021 update itself was not read; its content is taken from Bainum 2023. The clindamycin statement is supported (Brown 2013: highest odds of community-associated CDI, OR 16.80).

evidence.citation: Bainum TB, et al. Microorganisms. 2023;11(2):387
Gu T, et al. Front Cell Infect Microbiol. 2022;12:926482

flags.appAction: Lesson micro-result-to-therapy-mssa-cdi-giardia-flu teaches fidaxomicin as preferred by IDSA/SHEA and oral vancomycin as endorsed, with metronidazole limited.

flags.issue: Equates beta-lactamase-positive, oxacillin-susceptible S. aureus with MSSA without qualification. This is the phenotypic classification, and penicillinase does inactivate penicillin (Takayama 2018), but oxacillin-susceptible mecA-positive S. aureus (OS-MRSA) are reported: 11 of 74 ocular isolates in Brahma 2019 would have been misclassified as MSSA on susceptibility testing alone, and Andrade-Figueiredo 2016 found 30 phenotypic MSSA carrying mecA. Related to rv-oxacillin-s-mecc (mecC).

flags.issue: Hit 7 (and the Number Vault row) state RPR >=1:32 raises neurosyphilis risk 11x in HIV+ and 6x in HIV-negative patients. CDC 2021 adds that CSF examination followed by neurosyphilis treatment on the basis of laboratory abnormalities has not been associated with improved clinical outcomes in the absence of neurologic signs, and for persons with HIV and primary/secondary syphilis reserves CSF examination for those with an abnormal neurologic examination.

flags.issue: Hit 6 gives a positive prick test as '>=3 mm mean wheal'. The European standard (Heinzerling 2013) measures the largest wheal diameter; WAO 2020 defines positive as at least 3 mm more than the diluent control, describes mean-diameter recording options and lists device-specific thresholds (>3 mm for some devices). The 'up to 1000-fold' concentration difference matches Heinzerling's 1:10-1:1000 but WAO says 10-1000-fold or more. The intradermal '1+ = 5-10 mm' grading was not verified.

flags.issue: Hit 2 gives a fixed absolute lymphocyte threshold (<1200/mm³) for T-cell deficiency and states normal is >1500/mm³ 'at any age'. Lymphocyte counts are strongly age-dependent: in one reference study of healthy children the 2.5th percentile was 2,309/µL at 2–12 months but 1,136/µL at 0–1 month and 1,226/µL at 7–18 years, so a single cut-off both misses infant lymphopenia and mislabels normal older children. The PIDTC 2022 SCID definitions state that all T-cell quantification should be interpreted against age-associated reference intervals; they use T-cell (not total lymphocyte) counts, with age-specific cut-offs for leaky/atypical SCID (<0.6 × 10⁹/L any age, <0.8 at 2–4 y, <1.0 under 2 y), and express naïve CD4 cells as a proportion (<20%) rather than a naïve CD4 <200 cut-off.

evidence.citation: Dvorak CC, et al. J Allergy Clin Immunol. 2023;151(2):539-546
Zhang L, et al. J Immunol Res. 2022;2022:5603566

flags.appAction: Lesson immuno-tcell-defects-digeorge-bls-was teaches age-specific interpretation and leaves the 1200/mm³ and naïve CD4 <200 thresholds pending.

flags.issue: Hit 7 says 'IgA high, IgM low' and 'only WAS has small platelets'. Microplatelets were present in only 53% of the Sullivan series, and normal or even large platelets have been reported; one cohort found MPV only non-significantly lower than in ITP and called MPV an unreliable diagnostic clue. X-linked thrombocytopenia, caused by mutations in the same WAS gene, is a milder allelic phenotype that also causes thrombocytopenia. The immunoglobulin pattern is variable and sources differ: one review gives low IgM with high IgA and IgE, another says IgG, IgM and IgA are often low with high IgE, and one cohort found IgA raised in only 36% and IgM low in 39%.

evidence.citation: Hosahalli Vasanna S, et al. J Multidiscip Healthc. 2021;14:3497-3512
Jin YY, et al. Front Immunol. 2019;10:1549
Buchbinder D, et al. Appl Clin Genet. 2014;7:55-66

flags.issue: Hit 9 says MHC class I deficiency (TAP-1/TAP-2) causes 'decreased CD8+'. A 2025 long-term cohort and its literature review state that total CD8 T-cell counts may be preserved while naïve CD8 cells are markedly reduced; in the cohort CD8 counts were reduced in only 3 of 11 patients. TAPBP (tapasin) and B2M defects are rarer further causes, HLA-ABC expression is typically 1–15% of normal, and presentation is typically recurrent sinopulmonary infection, bronchiectasis and granulomatous skin lesions in late childhood or adolescence.

evidence.citation: Haskologlu S, et al. Front Immunol. 2025;16:1675097

flags.appAction: Lesson immuno-tcell-defects-digeorge-bls-was teaches that total CD8 counts can be normal in MHC class I deficiency and that HLA-ABC flow cytometry is the clue.

flags.issue: Hit 12 glosses R = M/ΔM as 'peak mass divided by resolving power' and defines resolving power (FWHM) as the peak width at 50% of peak height. The formula is right but the gloss is not: ΔM is the peak width at half maximum height (FWHM), and m/Δm itself is called the resolving power by Deschamps 2023, with resolving power quoted as a FWHM value by Chong 2018. Authors use 'resolution' and 'resolving power' differently.

evidence.citation: Deschamps E, et al. Molecules. 2023;28(5):2061
Chong YK, et al. Comput Struct Biotechnol J. 2018;16:316-334

flags.issue: Hit 5 presents 'Orbitrap (2005)' as the gold standard for large biomolecules with nondestructive detection. The analyzer was invented and patented in 1999 (Deschamps 2023) and named in 2000; 2005 was the commercial launch of the LTQ Orbitrap (Makarov 2026). Deschamps 2023 reports higher resolution for FT-ICR and states that Orbitrap analyzers are preferred for proteins and proteoforms below 50 kDa, while FT-ICR instruments are used in native approaches above 100 kDa. Neither source calls the Orbitrap a gold standard or describes its detection as nondestructive; both describe image-current detection with Fourier transformation.

evidence.citation: Makarov A. Mass Spectrom Rev. 2026;45(6):1064-1086

flags.issue: Hit 4 gives the M-spike calculation (percent of total protein x total protein) and a fixed SPEP reference-range table without caveats. Open sources describe densitometric M-protein quantitation as semi-quantitative: results depend on gating (perpendicular drop vs tangent skimming, the latter unreliable in the alpha/beta regions), comigration with beta-region proteins, and spike size (LOQ about 2 g/L, accuracy falls below 10 g/L); the same method should be used serially within a laboratory. The numerical reference ranges were not verified in the sources read.

flags.issue: Hit 2 (and Exam Trap 1) states cardiac valve allografts need NO ABO/HLA matching for long-term function because they rely on nonviable connective tissue. Cryopreserved homografts retain living donor endothelial and dendritic cells expressing HLA class II, most recipients develop HLA antibodies, the immune response is linked to early degeneration, and in one paediatric series ABO mismatch and (in the HLA-typed subgroup) HLA-DR mismatch were associated with echocardiographic valve failure. Valves are usually implanted without HLA matching or immunosuppression (both are described as research directions), but 'nonviable' and 'no effect of matching on long-term function' are not supported.

Jahnukainen T, et al. Ann Transplant. 2019;24:454-460

flags.issue: Hit 3 (and the Number Vault/Memory Hook) gives corneal enucleation within 6 hours of death, storage at 4°C and transplantation within 48–72 hours. The 2–3 day window reflects the original M–K medium. Later hypothermic media at 2–6°C are typically used for 7–10 days (claimed maximum 14–16 days) with death-to-storage generally within 12 h; organ culture at 31–37°C allows up to 4–5 weeks with death-to-storage extended to 24–48 h.

evidence.citation: Pels E, Beele H, Claerhout I. Int Ophthalmol. 2008;28(3):155-163

flags.issue: Hit 3 states long-term (>10 yr) success >90% and ~10% rejected, mostly from vascularization. Despite topical steroid prophylaxis 20–30% of corneal recipients have at least one rejection episode within 5 years; in high-risk eyes rejection occurs in 30–60% and up to 70% fail within 10 years. Neovascularisation is one of several risk factors (regraft, pretransplant inflammation, raised IOP), and outcomes depend strongly on indication. Exam Trap 2's FANCY statement is broadly correct, but FANCY enrolled mixed normal- and high-risk indications and was underpowered, and HLA-matching efficacy in high-risk grafts remains undetermined.

flags.issue: Hit 12 states capillary Hb exceeds venous by ~3 g/dL (and RBC by ~0.5 ×10¹²/L). A systematic review of paired studies reports that most, but not all, find capillary Hb higher: in a large donor study most paired values differed by 1 g/dL or less, analyzer-based studies in children and neonates found capillary Hb about 2–3% higher, and a large survey and a large Irish donor study found venous Hb higher (survey mean difference 0.9 g/dL). A ~3 g/dL gap is not supported. A higher capillary RBC count is reported (direction only), but the ~0.5 ×10¹²/L magnitude was not verified.

evidence.citation: Neufeld LM, et al. Ann N Y Acad Sci. 2019;1450(1):172-189
Krleza JL, et al. Biochem Med (Zagreb). 2015;25(3):335-358
